<reason>Both sides were sharp, disciplined, and well-structured (clean Q1/Q2 and A1/A2 compliance). B landed the debate's most memorable frames ("hiring-day vs retirement day," "mechanism vs drafting flaws") and expertly stacked A's partial concessions. But B's route depended on two vulnerable moves: (1) conceding in B4.1 that "no deduction nudges him directly" and relocating the motion to "everyone else," which edges toward swapping the motion and conflicts with A's unanswered A1.6 mandate design for employers without plans; (2) claiming the employer match as the tax preference's output, conflating the baseline 401(k) structure with the marginal policy of increasing deductions — A's closing caught this. A also left B's fiscal-cost point entirely unanswered across five speeches. A's core comparative (dented balance vs pristine zero for the insecurity-defining worker, plus match capture and free escalation on the intensive margin) survived the exchange, and A answered both pressure questions directly with a coherent escalation-with-raises mechanism. A's clipped Rebuttal 2 is a minor execution cost, but the substance was intact. A made the debate slightly easier to decide on the motion as written.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 1 move that "design freedom is symmetric or it is nothing" — catching B's double standard in praising deduction caps while calling escalation "an admission," plus noting refundable credits flee the motion — combined with A's Pressure Q1, which forced B's costly B4.1 concession that no deduction moves the non-participant, the worker A made the center of the motion.</best_rebuttal>
